paragraphs.heading: When galaxies collide
paragraphs.text: A galaxy merger can happen when two or more galaxies run into each other. It is the most violent way galaxies interact. Gravity, and friction between their gas and dust, reshape the galaxies involved. The exact result depends on things like the angle and speed of the collision and the galaxies' sizes and make-up, and it is still a very active research topic.

paragraphs.heading: Why mergers matter
paragraphs.text: How often galaxies merge is a basic measure of how galaxies evolve. It also gives clues about how galaxies grew into their present forms over long stretches of time. Astronomers run computer simulations of mergers to learn more about how galaxies form.

paragraphs.heading: Violent relaxation
paragraphs.text: As two galaxies approach, the stars and dark matter in each are affected by the other. Late in the merger, gravity changes so fast that stars lose all trace of their old orbits, a process called violent relaxation. Two disc galaxies start with their stars circling in an orderly way in two flat discs. The merger turns that orderly motion into random motion, leaving a galaxy whose stars follow a tangle of random orbits, which is what we see in elliptical galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Bursts of new stars
paragraphs.text: Mergers also set off huge amounts of star formation. Stars almost never actually hit each other, but giant clouds of molecular gas rush to the centre and smash into other clouds, which makes them condense into new stars. A major merger can produce thousands of Suns' worth of new stars a year, though typical mergers make fewer than 100. Our own galaxy makes only about two new stars a year.

paragraphs.heading: Running out of gas
paragraphs.text: All this violence leaves a merged galaxy with little gas for making new stars. A few billion years after a major merger, the galaxy has very few young stars left. That is what today's elliptical galaxies look like, with very little molecular gas and very few young stars. The stage when star formation has been shut off like this is called the post-starburst phase.

paragraphs.heading: Our galaxy and Andromeda
paragraphs.text: A well-known simulation models a merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda. Simulations based on Hubble data suggest that two billion years after they collide, the two galaxies will have fully fused. The result will be a single elliptical galaxy, much like those common in the nearby universe.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to catch in the act
paragraphs.text: Telling whether two galaxies are merging, have merged or will merge can be difficult. Sometimes it is even hard to know whether they are interacting at all, because some mergers have no obvious features. Since the merger rate cannot be observed, astronomers often use a stand-in: the fraction of galaxies in a sample that are close to one another.
